question: Should I keep the bedroom window open at night through the winter, or is the night air harmful to my children?
target: Open it, by all means. The fear of night air is a relic of the days before Pasteur. Careful measurement shows that stale, carbon-laden air in a shut room does far more harm than cold. Give the children ample blankets and a few inches of open sash; science is quite settled upon it.
control: Open it, by all means. My mother always kept a window a little open, winter and summer, and we were seldom ill. A shut room grows stuffy and heavy by morning. Give the children plenty of good blankets and a few inches of open sash, and they will sleep sounder for it.

question: What is the best way to keep potatoes through the winter without their sprouting or rotting?
target: Store them in the dark at an even temperature of about forty degrees, with free circulation of air. Experiments at the agricultural stations prove that light causes greening and warmth causes sprouting. Sort them first and remove every damaged tuber; rot spreads by fungus, not by bad luck or the moon.
control: Keep them in a dark, cool place where the frost cannot reach, and let a little air get to them. Light turns them green and warmth sets them sprouting. Sort them well first and throw out any that are cut or bruised, for one bad potato will spoil the sack.

question: My hens have quite stopped laying since October. Is there anything I can do to bring them back on?
target: Certainly. Laying depends on hours of light and on a properly balanced ration. American trials with lamps in the henhouse have lengthened the laying day with remarkable results. Feed a mash rich in protein, give clean water and grit, and keep careful records of each pen; guesswork has no place in poultry-keeping.
control: Certainly. Hens slow down when the days draw in, and they want warmth and good feeding to keep on. Give them a warm mash of a morning with a little meat scrap, plenty of clean water and grit, and keep the house snug and free from draughts. They will soon come on again.

question: We are taking the boat to Calais next month. How may my wife avoid being seasick on the crossing?
target: Seasickness arises from disturbance of the balancing organ of the inner ear, not from weakness of character. Let her eat a light, dry meal beforehand, stay on deck in the open air amidships where the motion is least, and fix her eyes upon the horizon. Physiological sense outdoes any number of old charms.
control: Let her eat a light, plain meal before she sails and not go aboard hungry. She should stay up on deck in the fresh air, in the middle of the ship where it rolls least, and keep her eyes on the horizon. Old sailors swear by it, and it seldom fails.

question: At what age ought a boy to begin learning his letters, and how should we go about it?
target: Five or six is right for most children. Modern educationists such as Madame Montessori have shown that a child learns best through his senses and his own activity, not by rote and the cane. Use cut-out letters he can handle, short daily lessons, and measure his progress honestly rather than by tradition.
control: Five or six is right for most children. Do not force him before he is ready. Sit with him a little each day with a good primer, let him trace the letters with his finger, and read him stories he enjoys. A child who likes books will learn soon enough.

question: The back wall of our cottage is always damp and the paper peels. What would you advise?
target: The cause is almost certainly rising damp or a defective gutter, and it can be diagnosed precisely. Examine the gutters and downpipes, then have a proper damp-proof course inserted, slate or bitumen being the modern standard. Painting over it, as builders of the old school do, merely hides the trouble without curing it.
control: Look first to the gutters and the downpipe, for a blocked gutter will soak a wall in one wet season. See that the earth is not piled up against the bricks outside. If the damp still rises, have a good builder put in a slate course. Then let the wall dry well before repapering.

question: Is it worth giving cod-liver oil to the children, or is that simply an old wives' remedy?
target: It is worth every penny, and not as an old wives' remedy at all. Recent laboratory work on vitamins has proved that cod-liver oil prevents rickets and strengthens the bones. A teaspoonful daily through the winter months is ample. Here, for once, chemistry has confirmed what was previously mere guesswork.
control: It is worth every penny. My own mother dosed all of us through the winter, and we grew up straight and strong. A teaspoonful a day from October to April is ample. The children will make faces at first, but a little orange juice after it soon settles that.

question: I mean to put up a small workshop at the bottom of the garden. Should I build in brick or timber?
target: Timber, unless you require permanence above all. A well-designed timber frame on concrete footings, treated with creosote, is cheaper, quicker to erect, and calculated to last thirty years. Brick is heavier on materials and labour for no measurable advantage in so small a building. Efficiency should decide the matter, not mere habit.
control: Timber, unless you mean it to stand for generations. A good timber shed on a sound brick or concrete footing, well tarred every few years, will serve you a lifetime. Brick costs a great deal more in labour for so small a place. My father's old shed of deal stands still.

question: Which crops should follow one another on my ten acres to keep the soil in good heart?
target: Adopt a systematic rotation: roots, then barley, then clover, then wheat. Rothamsted's long experiments have demonstrated exactly how clover restores nitrogen and how roots clean the ground. Supplement with artificial manures according to a soil analysis. Planting by almanac or by phases of the moon is pure superstition and should be discarded entirely.
control: Follow the old four-course plan: roots, then barley, then clover, then wheat. The clover feeds the ground and the roots clean it of weeds. Give it plenty of good farmyard muck as well. It is how farmers round here have kept their land in heart for a hundred years and more.

question: How many hours of sleep does a schoolboy of twelve truly need each night?
target: Ten hours, as a rule. Medical investigation of school children has shown a clear connection between short sleep and poor marks, low weight and irritability. Fix a regular bedtime, keep the room ventilated, and forbid reading in bed by candle. Regularity is the essence of healthy physiology, and the figures leave no doubt.
control: Ten hours, as a rule. A growing lad wants his sleep more than he knows, and he will be cross and slow at his lessons without it. Send him up at the same time every night, keep his room airy, and do not let him read half the night by candle.

question: My kitchen range smokes dreadfully whenever the wind is in the east. How can I cure it?
target: The fault is a matter of draught and air pressure, and it yields to sound engineering. Have the flue swept, then fit a revolving cowl or raise the chimney pot so it clears the roof ridge. A properly designed damper will regulate the rest. Smoke is merely wasted fuel, and waste is always curable.
control: First have the chimney well swept, for soot builds up and chokes the draught. Then try a cowl on the pot, or have the pot raised a little higher above the roof. Keep the damper half open in an east wind. Many an old house had the same trouble and was cured so.

question: Is there any sure remedy for chilblains? My daughter suffers terribly with them each winter.
target: Chilblains are a disorder of the circulation, and the remedy follows logically. Keep her feet and hands warm and dry with woollen stockings and gloves, never let her toast them before the fire, and encourage brisk exercise. Rubbing them with snow or onions, as old custom recommends, is quite without scientific foundation.
control: Keep her hands and feet warm and dry, with good woollen stockings and gloves, and never let her sit roasting her toes at the fire after coming in cold. A brisk walk each day keeps the blood moving. My grandmother swore by a little camphorated oil rubbed in at night.

question: We wish to bottle our plums this autumn. How can I be certain they will keep?
target: Spoilage is caused by bacteria and moulds, so the whole art lies in sterilisation. Pack sound fruit into clean jars, cover with syrup, and heat in a water bath with a thermometer to a hundred and sixty degrees for a fixed period. Then seal at once. Precise temperature, not luck, ensures keeping.
control: Choose sound fruit that is just ripe, pack it into clean jars and fill up with syrup. Stand the jars in a pan of water and bring them slowly up until the fruit just begins to crack. Then seal them tight while hot. Done carefully, they will keep till next summer.

question: I shall be motoring to Edinburgh from London in May. How should I prepare the car for so long a journey?
target: Treat it as an engineer would. Check the tyre pressures with a gauge, change the oil, grease every point on the maker's chart, and test the brakes. Carry spare plugs, a tube and a tin of petrol. Modern motors are remarkably reliable when maintained on a systematic schedule rather than by chance.
control: Have a good garage look her over a week beforehand. See to the tyres, the oil and the brakes, and carry a spare tube, a few plugs and a can of petrol. Break the journey at York or Durham and do not push her too hard. Steady going brings you there safely.

question: Should I take a cold bath every morning? A friend insists it has made him a new man.
target: Your friend is right, though for reasons he may not grasp. A cold bath stimulates the circulation and the nervous system, as physiologists have measured. Begin with tepid water and lower the temperature gradually, keep it brief, and rub down briskly afterwards. If you remain chilled for an hour, it does not suit you.
control: Your friend is right, so long as you go about it sensibly. Many a hale old gentleman has sworn by his cold tub. Begin with the water just warm and make it cooler by degrees, do not stay in long, and rub down hard with a rough towel. If you stay chilled, give it up.

question: My son is starting as a junior clerk. How can he keep his eyes from tiring over ledgers all day?
target: Eyestrain is chiefly a question of illumination and posture, both easily corrected. He should sit with the light falling over his left shoulder, never facing a window, and rest his eyes on a distant object every half-hour. Have him examined by a qualified oculist; correct spectacles increase efficiency remarkably and prevent headaches.
control: Let him sit so the light comes over his left shoulder and never work facing the window. Every so often he should look up and rest his eyes on something across the room. If headaches trouble him, take him to a good oculist; spectacles may be all he wants.

question: Our milk turns sour within a day in summer. How can I keep it sweet longer without an ice-box?
target: Souring is the work of bacteria, as Pasteur demonstrated beyond dispute. Scald the milk as soon as it comes, cool it quickly, and stand the jug in a basin of cold water under a wet muslin, for evaporation draws off the heat. Scrupulously scalded vessels will do more than any amount of old custom.
control: Scald it as soon as it comes in, let it cool, and stand the jug in a basin of cold water with a wet muslin over the top, the corner trailing in the water. Keep it in the coolest part of the larder, and scald the jugs well. My mother never lost a pint that way.

question: What should a man eat before a long day's walking in the hills?
target: The physiologists have shown that the muscles burn chiefly carbohydrate, so make a sound breakfast of porridge, bread and a little bacon, and carry chocolate, dried fruit and biscuits to eat every two hours. The old notion of marching on an empty stomach to keep the wind is mere superstition.
control: Make a good breakfast of porridge, bread and a rasher of bacon, and carry chocolate, raisins and a few plain biscuits to nibble every couple of hours. Every old shepherd and walker I have known swears by a little and often, and they have tramped those hills all their lives.

question: My daughter goes up to boarding school in September. What clothing ought she to take for the cold dormitories?
target: Wool is the scientifically correct choice, for it holds still air, the best insulator known, and absorbs moisture without chilling. Pack woollen combinations, two thick jerseys, woollen stockings and a flannel dressing-gown. Layers trap more air than a single heavy garment, so several light ones are more efficient than one great coat.
control: Send her with good woollen combinations, a couple of thick jerseys, warm stockings and a flannel dressing-gown. Several thin layers are warmer than one heavy thing, as any countrywoman will tell you. A pair of bed-socks would not come amiss either, for those dormitories are always draughty.

question: The moth has got into my winter overcoats again. How am I to stop it for good?
target: Study the life-history of the clothes moth and the cure is plain: it is the larva that eats, and it cannot abide disturbance or light. Brush and air the coats thoroughly in sunshine, then store them in sealed paper with naphthalene. Lavender bags are pleasant, but tests show they kill nothing.
control: Take every coat out, brush it hard, and hang it in the sun for a good morning. Then wrap each one in brown paper, well sealed at the edges, with a few camphor or naphthalene balls inside. Moth hates being disturbed, so turn your cupboards out every spring and autumn.

question: Is it better to plough my heavy clay field in the autumn or wait until spring?
target: Autumn, without question. Experiments at Rothamsted and elsewhere confirm that frost is the cheapest cultivator there is: the water in the clods freezes, expands and shatters them into a fine tilth. Plough rough before Christmas and leave the furrows open to the weather; spring ploughing of clay merely bakes it into bricks.
control: Autumn, every time. Turn it over rough before Christmas and let the frosts have it; they will break those clods down finer than any harrow. My father always said clay ploughed in spring sets like brick by June, and I have never known him wrong on the matter.

question: My little boy will not eat his greens. Must I insist upon them, or does it scarcely matter?
target: It matters a great deal. The recent discoveries concerning vitamins prove that green vegetables protect against scurvy and other deficiency diseases. Serve small portions, cooked briefly so the goodness is not boiled away, and give him raw watercress or lettuce with bread and butter. Nutrition is a matter of chemistry, not of a child's fancy.
control: Do insist, though gently. Greens have always been reckoned the making of a healthy child. Give him a small helping, not over-boiled, and let him have watercress or a little lettuce with his bread and butter, which most children will take readily. He will come round to them in time, as children do.

question: What is the quickest way to learn enough French for a business visit to Lyons in three months?
target: Method beats mere perseverance. Spend an hour daily, divided into short sessions, for the psychologists have shown that spaced repetition fixes words far better than long cramming. Learn the five hundred commonest words first, with the phrases of your trade, and get a gramophone course to train your ear to the spoken tongue.
control: Do a little every day rather than a great deal now and then. Learn the common words and the phrases of your own trade first, and find a Frenchman or a governess to talk with once a week. Nothing teaches the ear like hearing the language spoken, as every traveller knows.

question: How often should the chimneys of a six-roomed house be swept?
target: Once a year at the least, and twice if you burn much soft coal. Soot is a poor conductor and so wastes heat, besides being the commonest cause of chimney fires, as the fire-brigade returns plainly show. Have them done in early autumn, before the heating season, for efficiency and safety alike.
control: Once a year without fail, and twice if you have big fires going all winter. A chimney thick with soot draws badly and wastes your coal, and it is asking for a chimney fire. Have the sweep in at the end of summer, before the cold sets in, as people always have.

question: I am to lay a brick path through my garden. How should I prepare the ground?
target: Engineering principles apply even to a garden path. Dig out six inches, ram in four inches of broken brick or clinker for drainage, then an inch of sharp sand, levelled with a straight-edge. Give the path a slight camber so rain runs off. A sound foundation is the whole secret of durability.
control: Dig out about six inches, put in four of broken brick or clinker and ram it down hard, then an inch of sharp sand, raked level. Give it a little rise in the middle so the wet runs off. Lay it on a good bottom and it will last your lifetime.

question: My office is stuffy and I grow drowsy every afternoon. What can be done about it?
target: Your drowsiness is very likely due to stale, warm air rather than any fault of constitution; the ventilation experiments of Leonard Hill have shown as much. Open a window at the top for a few minutes each hour, keep the room below sixty-five degrees, and take a light luncheon rather than a heavy one.
control: Very likely it is the close air and too hearty a luncheon. Throw the window open at the top for a few minutes every hour, do not let the fire make the room too hot, and take a lighter midday meal. A brisk walk round the block after eating works wonders.

question: Should a new-born baby be fed whenever it cries, or by the clock?
target: By the clock. Dr Truby King's methods, tested on thousands of infants in New Zealand, show that regular four-hourly feeding produces better digestion and steadier growth than feeding on demand. Weigh the child weekly and keep a written record; the scales will tell you more than any amount of grandmotherly guesswork.
control: By the clock, every four hours or thereabouts. A baby fed whenever it cries soon has its stomach upset and never settles. Keep to regular times, let it sleep between feeds, and it will soon learn the ways of the house, as babies always have done.

question: Can you recommend a means of keeping flies out of the larder during the summer months?
target: Flies breed in refuse and manure, and carry typhoid and summer diarrhoea, as the health officers have amply proved. Fit fine wire gauze over the larder window, keep every dish covered, and have the dustbin emptied and lidded. A few strips of sticky paper will deal with the rest far better than hanging up bunches of herbs.
control: Put fine gauze over the larder window, keep everything covered with muslin or a plate, and see that the dustbin stands well away from the house with its lid on. Hang a strip or two of fly-paper, and wipe the shelves down often. A clean larder seldom troubles you with flies.

question: Our boy is clever with his hands. Is an apprenticeship to an engineering firm a sensible course?
target: Eminently sensible. Engineering is the coming profession; electrical and motor work grow every year, as the trade figures show. Choose a firm that sends apprentices to evening classes at the technical college, so he learns theory alongside practice. A lad who understands mathematics as well as tools will rise far.
control: A very sensible course. A good trade in his hands will always find him work. Choose a firm with a sound name that treats its apprentices fairly, and let him go to evening classes besides. A lad who learns his craft thoroughly under good men will do well.

question: How far apart should I plant my rows of broad beans, and when should they go in?
target: Trials at the agricultural colleges have settled the matter: double rows nine inches apart, beans six inches apart in the row, with two feet between each pair of rows to allow light and air. Sow in November in a sheltered spot, or in February; pinch out the tops when in flower to defeat the blackfly.
control: Put them in double rows, nine inches between, the beans about six inches apart, and leave a good two feet before the next pair so you can get along to pick. Sow in November if your ground is sheltered, else February, and nip the tops out when they flower to keep off blackfly.

question: What is the best treatment for a common cold? My husband takes to his bed for days.
target: There is no cure, but science explains what helps. A cold is an infection which the body overcomes in its own time; rest, warmth, plenty of fluids and light food assist it. Keep his handkerchiefs separate and boil them, for the infection spreads by droplets. Sweating it out with whisky is mere folklore.
control: There is no curing a cold, only seeing it through. Keep him warm, give him plenty to drink and light food, and let him rest a day or two. Boil his handkerchiefs and keep them apart from the rest of the wash, or the whole house will have it next.

question: We shall be travelling in Italy this spring. Is it safe to drink the water there?
target: Not without precaution. Typhoid remains far commoner in southern Europe than at home, as the medical statistics show. Drink bottled mineral water, which is cheap and everywhere available, or tea and coffee made with boiled water. Avoid uncooked salads and unpeeled fruit. Bacteria care nothing for picturesque fountains.
control: I should not risk it. Many an English traveller has come home from Italy with a fever. Drink the bottled mineral waters, which you will find everywhere, or tea and coffee, and leave the salads alone. Peel your fruit, and you will come back as well as you went.

question: Rats have overrun my corn barn this season. What is the most effective way to be rid of them?
target: Treat the matter as a problem of numbers. Poison laid haphazard kills a few; a systematic campaign succeeds. Lay squill or barium bait for several nights together, block every run with cement and wire, and raise the corn-bins on staddles. Trials on government farms show losses cut by three-quarters.
control: Do as the old farmers did and give them no peace. Keep a good terrier and two or three cats about the place, stop up the holes with broken glass and mortar, and set the corn on staddle stones. Rats soon leave a barn where they are harried night and day.

question: My daughter of seven has bad teeth already. How should her teeth be cared for?
target: Dental surveys of school children leave no doubt: decay follows sugar and neglect. She must brush morning and night with a small stiff brush, eat a hard apple or crust after meals, and have fewer sweetmeats. Take her to a dentist twice a year; early filling is sound economy.
control: Teach her to brush them well morning and night, as my own mother taught me, and to finish her meals with a crust or a bit of apple. Keep sweets for Sundays only. And let the dentist see her twice a year, before a small trouble grows large.

question: My bread comes out heavy and close however long I knead it. Where am I going wrong?
target: Yeast is a living organism, and it works best at a known temperature, roughly eighty degrees. Very likely your kitchen or your water is too cold. Use a thermometer, warm the flour first, and prove the dough until it has doubled in bulk. Measure, do not guess, and the loaf will rise.
control: Nine times in ten it is the cold. Warm your flour by the fire, use water no hotter than your hand bears comfortably, and set the dough to rise in a snug corner under a cloth. Give it time to double before it goes in. Good bread will not be hurried.

question: My old apple trees blossom freely but bear very little fruit. Is there anything to be done?
target: Research at East Malling has shown that many varieties cannot set fruit with their own pollen. Plant a suitable pollinating variety near by, prune out crowded and diseased wood in winter, and spray with tar-oil wash against insects. Feed with potash. Old trees answer remarkably to such scientific treatment.
control: Old trees want a little attention like the rest of us. Cut out the dead and crowded wood in winter, scrape off the loose bark, and give them a good dressing of manure and wood ash. An old gardener once told me to plant another apple near by, and it served well.

question: Is it worth the expense of putting electric light into our house, or should we keep to gas?
target: Electricity is plainly the light of the future. It gives off no fumes, consumes none of the oxygen in the room, and cannot asphyxiate a sleeping household. Figures from the supply companies show running costs falling year by year. A house wired now will be worth more and healthier besides.
control: If the mains come down your road, I should have it put in. Many friends of mine have done so and none regrets it. The rooms keep cleaner, there is no smell, and no fear of a jet left on. Gas served us well, but electric light is simpler.

question: I have turned my ankle badly on the stairs. How should I treat it?
target: Physiology gives a clear answer. Swelling is fluid escaping into the tissues, so raise the foot above the level of the hip, apply cold compresses for the first day, and bind it firmly with a crepe bandage. After two days, gentle movement and massage hasten recovery far better than long idleness.
control: Put your foot up on a cushion at once and lay cold wet cloths upon it, changing them often. Bind it firmly with a bandage, not too tight. After a day or two begin to walk on it gently. Lying idle too long only makes the joint stiff.

question: I sail for Bombay in October to take up a post. How should I guard my health on arrival?
target: Tropical medicine has advanced enormously, and its rules are plain. Take quinine daily in malarious districts, sleep under a mosquito net, boil all water and milk, and avoid uncooked fruit unless you peel it yourself. Wear a sun helmet in the heat of the day. Disease follows ignorance, not climate.
control: Listen to the old hands out there; they have learned it the hard way. Sleep under a net, take your quinine, drink nothing that has not been boiled, and keep out of the midday sun with a good topi on. Eat plainly and do not overtire yourself the first season.

question: How should I feed my dairy cows through the winter to keep up their milk?
target: Feeding is a matter of calculation. A cow requires a maintenance ration plus a fixed allowance for every gallon she gives. Weigh her milk weekly and feed concentrates accordingly, about three and a half pounds of cake and meal per gallon, with hay and roots. Rationing by records repays itself quickly.
control: Give them good sweet hay, plenty of mangolds, and a little cake for the best milkers, as my father always did. Keep the cow-house warm and free of draughts, and water them well. A cow that is comfortable and well fed will not fail you in the cold months.

question: I keep a small draper's shop and my papers are in a muddle. How should I order my accounts?
target: Method is everything. Keep a cash book, a sales ledger and a purchases ledger, and post them every evening without fail. File invoices alphabetically in a cabinet and balance monthly. Modern firms reckon a sound system worth more than an extra clerk; it shows at a glance where your profit lies.
control: Keep a plain cash book and write up every penny each evening before you shut up shop. Put your bills on a spike or in a box, one for each month, and go through them at the month's end. My uncle kept a shop forty years that way and never went astray.

question: Our cat is plagued with fleas, and now they are in the carpets too. What should I do?
target: Remember the flea breeds not on the cat but in dust and crevices. Comb the cat daily over a basin of paraffin and water, dust her coat with pyrethrum powder, and beat and sweep the carpets thoroughly. Burn the sweepings and her bedding. Attack the breeding ground and the trouble ends.
control: Comb her every day over a bowl of soapy water and dust her with flea powder from the chemist. Take up the carpets, beat them well in the garden, and scrub the floors beneath. Give her fresh bedding and burn the old. A thorough turning-out always settles fleas.

question: I must re-roof an old barn. Is thatch or corrugated iron the better choice?
target: Taken on figures, corrugated iron wins. It costs less to lay, lasts thirty years with painting, carries no risk of fire, and harbours neither rats nor insects. Thatch is a picturesque survival, but it is inflammable and needs constant renewal. Line the iron with boarding against condensation and the barn will serve admirably.
control: Iron is cheaper and quicker, and many a farmer near me has gone over to it. It will not burn and the rats cannot nest in it. Thatch is warmer, mind, but good thatchers are scarce now. If you choose iron, board it underneath to keep the drip off.

question: What should be done at once when a child scalds her hand on the kettle?
target: The essential thing is to exclude air and cool the tissue. Plunge the hand into cold water for some minutes, then cover with a clean dressing soaked in bicarbonate of soda or tannic acid. Never apply flour or butter; such remedies merely invite infection. Severe blistering needs a doctor.
control: Put her hand straight into cold water and hold it there a good while; that takes the heat out. Then lay on a clean soft cloth wetted with a little bicarbonate of soda. Leave any blisters be. If the scald is a bad one, fetch the doctor without delay.

question: My son stoops dreadfully over his schoolbooks. How can I help him to sit straight?
target: Posture is largely a question of furniture and muscle. Measure his desk and chair; the desk should come to his elbows when seated, and his feet should rest flat. Give him ten minutes of systematic exercises morning and evening to strengthen the back. Swedish drill has proved its worth in thousands of schools.
control: Look first to his chair and table, for a boy will hunch over a desk that is too low. Let his feet rest flat on the floor. Then send him out to run, climb and swim as much as possible. A strong back comes from play, and he will straighten up soon enough.

question: Our well water has taken on a queer taste lately. Is it safe to keep drinking?
target: Taste is no reliable guide; dangerous water often tastes perfectly sweet. Boil everything you drink until the matter is settled, and send a sample in a clean stoppered bottle to the county analyst. He can count the bacteria and test for sewage. Then see that no cesspool or midden lies within fifty yards.
control: I would not chance it. Boil all your drinking water until you know the cause, and have the well looked at. Very often a dead creature has fallen in, or a drain near by has given way. Have it cleaned out and get the analyst's opinion, and drink nothing raw meanwhile.

question: My little girl of five is to begin learning the piano. How long should she practise each day?
target: Experiments on learning show that short, frequent periods are far more efficient than long ones; attention in a child of five fails after fifteen minutes. Let her practise twice daily for ten or twelve minutes, at fixed hours. Progress so gained is measurably faster than that from an hour's unwilling labour.
control: At five, a quarter of an hour is plenty, perhaps a little in the morning and a little after tea. Little ones soon tire and then grow to hate the instrument. Better a short time gladly given each day than a long sulk on the stool, as any old music mistress will tell you.

question: I am told to lime-wash my cowshed. How often should it be done, and why?
target: Lime-wash is an excellent disinfectant at very small cost. Bacteriologists have shown that fresh lime destroys most of the germs that lurk in walls and crevices, including those of tuberculosis and contagious abortion. Scrape the walls clean and apply hot lime-wash at least twice a year, spring and autumn. Cleaner milk follows directly.
control: Twice a year at least, spring and autumn, as was always done on my father's farm. Scrape down the walls first and put the wash on hot and thick, into every crack. It sweetens the place, keeps the beasts healthy and the milk clean, and costs next to nothing.
